visits.text: Road from Essaouira to Agadir along the Atlantic coast: argan trees appear shortly after Essaouira - it's one of the rare places in the world where these trees grow, and goats climbing their branches to eat the fruit are an authentic spectacle (not staged, unlike certain tourist spots). The argan forest is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

The Kasbah of Agadir Oufella, perched on a hill 236 m above the bay, is the only vestige from before the 1960 earthquake that destroyed the city in 15 seconds. The view from the summit sweeps the entire Bay of Agadir, its 9 km beach, and the Souss mountains behind. The drive or walk up is worth the trip.

Souss Massa National Park, created in 1991 between Agadir and Tiznit, extends across 33,800 hectares of coastal cliffs, dunes, wetlands, and steppes. The Oued Massa estuary is a Ramsar site of international importance for migratory birds: on the 5 km walking circuit, you'll observe flamingos, spoonbills, gray herons, cormorants, and - if you're lucky - the northern bald ibis, one of the world's most threatened species with 95% of the wild population nesting here. Binoculars recommended.

The town of Tiznit, 90 km south of Agadir, is known for its medina ringed by 7 km of pink ramparts and for its silversmiths - the town is Morocco's main center of Berber jewelry. Place du Méchouar and its blue spring are the quiet heart of the old town.

activities.text: Stroll through Souk El Had: 6,000 shops on several levels, spices, textiles, leather, fruit and vegetables. It is a local market, not a tourist market - prices are displayed and there is less pressure than in Marrakech.

4x4 circuit in the park's animal reserves (Rokein and Arrouis): addax with long horns, dorcas gazelles, scimitar oryx, and red-necked ostrich - species extinct in the wild in Morocco and reintroduced here since the 1990s. Visits are mandatory with a park guide.

visits.text: You will cross Tizi n'Tinififft Pass, at an elevation of 1,660 m, on the road from Ouarzazate to Agdz. From the viewpoint, you can see the arid Saghro Mountains, almost devoid of vegetation. The road then descends toward the first palm groves of the Drâa Valley, which begins at Agdz. Stop at the pass for 15 minutes to take in the contrast between the dry rock and the green ribbon of the palm grove.

The Caïd Ali Kasbah overlooks Agdz from a rocky promontory. This 19th-century fortified residence, built of unfired earth bricks, belonged to the caïd, the local governor. Inside, a maze of rooms leads up to the terraces. The building is largely abandoned and belongs to the caïd's descendants: speak with them on-site to arrange a visit.

“Meeting place” is the meaning of Tamnougalt in Tachelhit, the Amazigh (Berber) language of southern Morocco. This ksar, 6 km from Agdz on the other side of the Drâa, was the capital of the Mezguita, the tribe that dominated this part of the valley. Its caïds lived in the Kasbah of the Caïds: three levels of rammed earth surrounding a courtyard, with painted wooden ceilings and carved plasterwork. Some rooms are fragile, so ask before entering. Hire a guide to explore the covered lanes and the former Jewish quarter.

activities.text: In the shade of the date palms in the Agdz palm grove, water flows through seguias, small open-air irrigation channels. They distribute water among plots of henna, mint, and fig trees. Paths connect the douars, the hamlets scattered throughout the palm grove. Set out in the morning with a local guide: they will show you how water flows from one garden to the next and may be able to arrange tea in a local home.

If you are in Agdz on a Thursday, set aside 1 hour for the souk, the weekly market where people from neighboring villages come to sell goods and stock up. Spices, dates, and olives fill the stalls, while the butchers occupy a separate area. This is no tourist market, but part of everyday life in the valley. Come in the morning, before the intense heat.

visits.text: Ochre earthen houses stacked up to the top of a hill: the ksar of Aït-Ben-Haddou looks like a movie set, and it has often served as one. This fortified earthen village, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, appears in Lawrence of Arabia, Gladiator, and the series Game of Thrones. Only a few families still live here. Most residents have settled on the other side of the Ounila River, which runs alongside the ksar: cross it using the pedestrian bridge completed in 2011.

If you still have energy after exploring the narrow streets, climb to the agadir crowning the hill of Aït-Ben-Haddou. This former fortified granary protected the entire village's harvests; only its walls remain. From the summit, the view stretches across the Ounila Valley and the ksar's terrace rooftops. Wear sturdy shoes, as the earthen steps are uneven, and head down before nightfall to return to Ouarzazate, about 30 kilometers away.

visits.text: Al Hoceima is a young city: the Spanish founded it in the 1920s under the name Villa Sanjurjo. A Catholic church from the colonial era still stands in the center. Spanish remains widely spoken here. In the evening, head to Mohammed VI Square. Its ground-level fountains light up at nightfall.

Walk down to Quemado Beach, a few minutes from central Al Hoceima. This is the city beach, just 300 m long. In summer, pedal boats are available for rent, and the beach fills up very quickly. In the off-season, you are more likely to see fishermen bringing in their catch. Come early in the morning to enjoy it while it is quiet.

The best time to stroll around Al Hoceima’s port is late in the day. The Moroccan tourist office recommends walking here to watch the fishermen at work. It is the Rif’s second port after Nador. Ferries also connect it to Motril, Spain. Watch out for ropes and crates: this is a working port, not a marina.

The sand at Sfiha Beach is black, and three islets dot the horizon. One of them, Peñón de Alhucemas, has a fortress and remains under Spanish sovereignty. The 2 km beach belongs to the municipality of Ajdir, the birthplace of Abdelkrim el-Khattabi. This leader from the Rif fought the Spanish army and proclaimed the Republic of the Rif in 1921. In summer, the official count records up to 10,000 swimmers a day: come early.

If Quemado is packed, head to Cala Bonita, another of the city’s beaches. This cove is tucked into a bay enclosed by rocky cliffs. Access is down a few steps, making it less convenient with a stroller. Bring water and a beach umbrella, and arrive early to choose your spot.

activities.text: After 6 p.m., buy your fish directly from the boats docked at Al Hoceima’s port. Then have it grilled at the Club nautique restaurant, the best-known restaurant in the port. Its upper floor overlooks the entire port, making it an ideal place to end the trip in peace. Ask how much grilling costs before ordering.

The coastline of Al Hoceima National Park is best seen from the sea. Small boats leave the port to cruise along the coast. The park is home to a large concentration of ospreys, large birds of prey that dive to catch fish. Negotiate the price and duration before boarding, and bring a windbreaker.

visits.text: Anemiter is worth stopping for: its ksar, a fortified village with earthen walls, is one of the best preserved in Morocco. It lies about 15 kilometers from Télouet, at the start of the Ounila Valley. The painter Jacques Majorelle stayed here in 1921. Park at the top of the village and walk down into the old ksar: the track leading to it is in poor condition.

Though half in ruins, Tamdaght’s kasbah served as the setting for a major scene in director Ridley Scott’s film Gladiator. From Anemiter, plan a round-trip drive through the Ounila Valley to reach Tamdaght. A kasbah is the fortified residence of a prominent family. This one belonged to the Glaoui family, as did the palace in Télouet. Some rooms are no longer accessible. There is no ticket booth or opening hours: knock on the door to ask to enter.

activities.text: You will then head down the Ounila Valley on the P1506, a paved road suitable for a regular car. For about 40 kilometers, the Ounila River traces a ribbon of green farmland between ocher canyons. This valley was a route for caravans carrying salt and goods from the Sahara. Look out for cave dwellings carved into the rock, which served as shelters during conflicts. Without stops, the most scenic stretch takes 1 hour 30 minutes to drive.

visits.text: House upon house, Aroumd rises on a large moraine spur—a mass of rocks and earth left behind by an ancient glacier. At about 1,900 m, it is the highest village in the Aït Mizane Valley, around forty minutes on foot from Imlil. Below, terraces irrigated for a very long time produce barley, corn, and vegetables. The narrow lanes all look alike, making it easy to get lost, so follow the main path or ask for directions.

activities.text: If your legs are up to it, climb from Aroumd to the shrine of Sidi Chamharouch, at 2,350 m, on the Toubkal trail. Allow about two hours for the ascent, with a steep first half, and three to four hours round-trip from Aroumd. You will know you have arrived when you see tea stalls beside the stream, near a small waterfall. The shrine is a pilgrimage site closed to non-Muslims: view it from a distance. A licensed guide is mandatory for this hike on the Toubkal trail.

visits.text: Few Moroccan medinas are as peaceful as Asilah’s. A medina is a fortified old town, and this one is entirely pedestrian. Its ramparts were built by the Portuguese, who captured the city on August 24, 1471. Enter through Bab al-Homer, the Land Gate, and leave through Bab al-Bahr, the Sea Gate. Right beside it, Borj al-Bahr, a bastion completed in 1516, projects into the ocean.

Borj al-Kamra, the main tower in Asilah’s ramparts, rises above Sidi Ali ben Hamdouch Square. It dates to 1509. The Portuguese called it Torre de Menagem, meaning the keep: the strongest tower, where people retreated during an attack. Walk around this massive square structure, then use the square as a meeting point that is easy to find in the medina.

The walls of Asilah’s medina are white, but their appearance changes every year. Since 1978, the Asilah International Cultural Moussem, a festival founded by painter Mohamed Melehi and mayor Mohamed Benaïssa, has had new murals painted on houses each year. The festival includes a summer session and a fall session, with concerts and exhibitions depending on the program. Wander without a route in mind, camera in hand: every alley may reveal a recent mural.

A former bandit had this palace built beside the ocean. Raissouni Palace dates to 1909 and is named after Moulay Ahmed er-Raissouni, the tribal chief who had kidnapped Ion Perdicaris five years earlier. Its reception room combines zellige (a mosaic of small glazed tiles), stucco (carved plasterwork), and painted wood. A terrace overlooks the ocean. Now a cultural center, it opens for exhibitions and events during the Cultural Moussem: at other times, view its facade from the ramparts.

Tombs covered in colorful ceramics descend toward the ocean in Asilah’s seaside cemetery. Walk discreetly along the edge of this Muslim cemetery, without walking between the graves. The overlook above it offers an unobstructed view of the setting sun, with the Atlantic as a backdrop. Arrive half an hour before sunset to find a good spot.

activities.text: If Asilah’s main beach feels too urban, drive south to Rmilat Beach, nicknamed Paradise Beach. This 5 km stretch of sand is wilder than the town beach. The official beach information sheet lists no drinking water supply, so bring water and a beach umbrella.

visits.text: Ochre ramparts overlook a slow-moving river: Azemmour’s medina lines the left bank of the Oum Er-Rbia. The Portuguese occupied it from 1513 to 1541. Estevanico, a native of the city who had been enslaved, left in 1527 with a Spanish expedition to North America. He was one of four survivors out of several hundred men. Today, many walls display murals, portraits, and calligraphy by Moroccan and foreign artists. Wander without a set route, camera in hand.

activities.text: The Oum Er-Rbia estuary begins just a few minutes from Azemmour’s medina. Wetlands, dunes, and green riverbanks attract migratory birds, and a few fishermen still practice traditional fishing here. Come late in the day to photograph the river, then get back on the road: El Jadida is only about twenty minutes away.

visits.text: Carved shells frame the arch of Bab Agnaou, cut from ocher-colored sandstone. Completed around 1190 under the Almohad caliph Yacoub al-Mansour, this gate was the main entrance to the royal kasbah, the sultan’s citadel. Above the arch runs a frieze in Kufic script, an angular form of Arabic calligraphy, featuring verses from the Quran. The meaning of its Berber name remains debated. Stop on the outside to read the frieze, then pass through the gate: the Saadian Tombs are a five-minute walk away.

visits.text: It looks very old, but Bab Bou Jeloud, the grand western gate of the medina of Fez, dates from 1913. The French administration built it as a ceremonial entrance. Its ceramic tiles are blue on the outside and green on the inside. Through the arch, you can already see the minaret of Bou Inania, the religious school you will visit next. Unlicensed guides often wait here. If you want a guide, hire an official one: they must show you their Ministry of Tourism ID. Agree in advance on the price, the route, and a “no shops” rule.

visits.text: Borj Nord kept watch over the enemies of Fez, as well as the city’s own inhabitants. Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour of the Saadian dynasty had this fort built in 1582 on a hill north of the medina. At the time, the people of Fez el-Bali were considered unruly, and the fort was also intended to keep them in check. Today, the fort houses an arms museum: cannons occupy two rooms, alongside sabers, daggers, and rifles. Look for the large firing platform, pierced with 56 openings for cannons. The museum is closed on Mondays.

visits.text: In 1904, the kidnapping of an American in this forest brought the United States Navy to Tangier. Perdicaris Park bears his name: Ion Perdicaris had a villa here, where tribal chief Raissouni kidnapped him on May 18, 1904. President Roosevelt sent seven warships to Tangier, and the hostage was released for a ransom. Since 2022, the restored villa has housed a heritage interpretation center. Afterward, take a walk through Rmilat Forest, overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar.

Cape Spartel marks the point where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea, 14 km west of Tangier. Its lighthouse was built in 1864 at the request of European consuls concerned about the many shipwrecks offshore. In 1865, ten foreign countries and Morocco signed an agreement to maintain it jointly. On a clear day, look across the water for Cape Trafalgar on the Spanish coast, 44 km away.

An opening onto the ocean traces the outline of Africa: this is the sight visitors come to see at the Caves of Hercules. Waves carved out these caves, and local people later enlarged them by cutting out millstones for oil presses. According to legend, Hercules rested here before going to pick the golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides. The ground is dark and slippery: wear sturdy shoes, and come early or in the late afternoon to avoid the crowds.

visits.text: Rabat is not on the road from Agadir: the city is about 87 km from Casablanca, 1 hour's drive north, and is visited as a round trip from Casablanca. The Hassan Tower, an unfinished 12th-century minaret, was meant to be the minaret of the largest mosque in the world according to the Almohad sultan Yacoub al-Mansour. His death in 1199 halted the work at 44 m - half the planned height. The 200 columns of the never-completed mosque now form a silent field of stone around the tower.

The Mausoleum of Mohammed V, facing the Hassan Tower, houses the tombs of King Mohammed V, architect of Morocco's independence, his son Hassan II, and Prince Moulay Abdallah. Built between 1961 and 1971 by 400 Moroccan artisans, its green-tiled pyramidal roof, white Italian marble, and zelliges make it a masterpiece of contemporary Moroccan art. Entry is free and open to non-Muslims.

The Kasbah des Oudayas, a 12th-century Almohad fortress on the Bouregreg estuary, dominates the river and Atlantic. Its blue and white alleys resemble a miniature Chefchaouen. Café Maure, inside the kasbah, is the place for mint tea facing the estuary.

The Hassan II Mosque, built over the sea between 1987 and 1993, is one of the largest mosques in the world, with its 210 m minaret. Its prayer hall can hold 25,000 worshippers, with a further 80,000 people on its esplanade.

Casablanca's downtown Art Deco quarter, built during the French protectorate (1920s-1950s), concentrates one of the world's most remarkable Art Deco architecture collections outside Miami. Place Mohammed V, with its fountains and arcades, is the center. Walk among facades ornamented with geometric forms and Moroccan motifs reinterpreted in concrete.

activities.text: The Chellah, 2 km from central Rabat, combines Roman vestiges of the ancient city of Sala Colonia (1st century) and a 14th-century Marinid necropolis in a garden invaded by storks nesting on the minarets. A historic monument since 1920 and UNESCO heritage since 2012, it's one of Morocco's most unusual sites.
Guided tour inside the Hassan II Mosque for non-Muslims: official providers offer organised tours in the morning and afternoon. Book ahead, places are limited.

Seafood lunch on the Corniche of Casablanca before departure: the waterfront, stretching from the port to Ain Diab, is lined with fish restaurants with terraces on the Atlantic. A final image of Morocco facing the ocean.

visits.text: Road from Tangier to Chefchaouen through the slopes of the Rif: the first mountain hairpins reveal the red tile roofs and first blue facades long before entering town. Late afternoon arrival recommended to catch the light in the medina.

Place Uta el-Hammam is the heart of Chefchaouen: sidewalk cafés, the Great Mosque with its 15th-century octagonal minaret, and the ochre-walled Kasbah built by Moulay Ali Ben Rachid, founder of the city in 1471. Inside the Kasbah, an ethnographic museum displays costumes, musical instruments, and pottery - climb the tower for views over the medina's blue rooftops from above.

The Spanish Mosque (Bouzaafar) is THE viewpoint of Chefchaouen: built in the 1920s during the protectorate but never used for worship, it's now the photographers' essential spot. Allow 25 to 30 minutes walking from Ras el-Maa. Arrive an hour before sunset - the medina shifts from brilliant blue to golden and orange tones as the sun descends behind the Rif ridges.

The Ras el-Maa spring, a few minutes from the medina, is Chefchaouen's natural breathing point: water descends from the mountains, women come to wash laundry, children play on the rocks. It's a scene of daily life worth more than many monuments.

activities.text: First stroll through the blue alleys at dusk. Chefchaouen's blue traces back to the Sephardic Jewish community that arrived from Spain after 1492 - they painted the walls to symbolize sky and the divine. Get lost in dead-end streets without trying to see everything: that's the best plan.

For those with energy, the excursion to Akchour waterfalls (30 km from Chefchaouen) is one of the region's most beautiful: natural pools, cedar forest, and the famous Bridge of God, a natural rock formation. Local operators organize shared taxi transfers from the main square.

Tour the artisan souks early morning - wool textiles with Berber patterns, rugs, and the town's signature blue pottery deserve a visit. Monday and Thursday, the local market sets up with farm products at local prices.

visits.text: More than 20,000 whitewashed graves cover Miâara Jewish Cemetery, the largest in Morocco. Near the entrance, some graves are painted blue. These belong to the Cohanim, descendants of the priests of the Temple in Jerusalem. Men, women, and children are buried in separate sections. One corner of the cemetery holds around 6,000 children who died during a typhus epidemic in the 19th century. Men are lent a kippah at the entrance, and a donation to the caretaker is customary. Avoid Saturdays and Jewish holidays.

visits.text: In 1910, Thami El Glaoui, the future pasha of Marrakech, meaning the city’s governor, commissioned Dar El Bacha. He wanted it to be luxurious enough to impress his guests. Since 2017, the palace has housed the Museum of Confluences, dedicated to Moroccan decorative arts and objects from other cultures. Its exhibitions change regularly. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the museum reopened as early as November of that year. It is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 AM to 6 PM and closed on Mondays. Expect to pay around 60 dirhams.

activities.text: Extend your visit at Bacha Coffee, the café set in a historic salon at Dar El Bacha. This café specializes in arabica, a variety of coffee bean. Reservations are not accepted, and a line may form at busy times. Coffee is charged separately, in addition to museum admission.

visits.text: In El Jadida, walk along the citadel that houses the Portuguese Cistern: its interior is closed for restoration and cannot be visited. This chamber, approximately 34 m on each side and supported by 25 pillars, may have served as an arsenal before becoming a water reservoir in 1541. Before the closure, a thin layer of water covered the floor and reflected the vaults. A shaft of light fell through a round opening that once collected rainwater. Orson Welles filmed a scene here for his Othello, released in 1952. Stay outside the construction site.

Next, you will climb a steep ramp onto the ramparts of Mazagan, the former Portuguese name for El Jadida. About 8 m high and 10 m thick, they have a 2 m-wide wall walk. The star-shaped fortress dates from 1541–1548, and UNESCO listed it in 2004. The Portuguese left in 1769: the empty city was nicknamed “the ruined one,” then renamed El Jadida, “the new one,” in the 19th century. From the Bastion of the Angel, the view stretches over the ocean and harbor.

The Sea Gate, at the end of the Portuguese city’s main street, is the old passage where ships unloaded their goods. Beneath a nearby arch, a communal oven still bakes bread brought by women from the neighborhood. Near the entrance, the Church of the Assumption is built in the Manueline style, the Portuguese Gothic style of the early 16th century. The Grand Mosque, right next door, has a five-sided minaret. Ask before photographing local residents at the oven.

visits.text: El Jebha means “the forehead” in Arabic: the Rif Mountains frame this small port like a forehead above the sea. Under the Spanish protectorate, the town was called Puerto Capaz. Its port shelters many fishing boats and also welcomes recreational boaters cruising along the coast. Walk around the docks before getting back on the road.

activities.text: If you pass through on a Tuesday, stop at El Jebha’s souk, one of the largest and liveliest in the region according to the Moon guide. A souk is a traditional market. On other days, head down to the 1.8 km sand-and-pebble beach at the mouth of the Ouringa, a small river. There are no showers or restrooms: bring water.

visits.text: Erg Chigaga is Morocco’s largest erg, a sea of sand dunes. It stretches for around 40 kilometers between Jbel Bani to the north and the hamada, a stony plateau, toward M’Hamid. Some dunes rise more than 50 m high. Until around 1990, this was a military zone, and few travelers came here. Even today, there are no roads or villages, only camps. Bring a warm jacket, as nights are cold even after a scorching day.

activities.text: Climb a large dune in Erg Chigaga an hour before sunset. Take your time: in soft sand, every step takes much more effort than it would on a trail. From the summit, the dunes’ shadows stretch eastward, and the silence is almost complete. Keep a headlamp handy for the descent, and locate the camp lights before night falls.

Slow, swaying, and a little hard on the back, a dromedary camel ride is still the most fitting way to experience Erg Chigaga. You can even reach the erg from M’Hamid on a multiday trek with a caravan. For a first experience, a one-hour ride from camp is enough. Request it when booking your desert camp stay, and wear long pants for greater comfort in the saddle.

With no villages for tens of kilometers around, Erg Chigaga’s night sky is dark enough to photograph the stars. The organized desert camp, a tent camp set up by a tour operator, provides dinner and sleeping accommodations. Before booking, ask how the camp manages water and waste: in such a dry environment, it matters. If possible, choose a date near the new moon, when the sky is darkest.

If you get up half an hour before dawn, you will see Erg Chigaga’s dunes turn from gray to pink, then gold. The morning sand is still cool and holds the tracks left overnight by small desert animals. Walk for an hour before breakfast, then pack your bag for the return trip by 4x4 to M’Hamid, where your car awaits.

visits.text: Beginning in 1760, French engineer Théodore Cornut designed part of Essaouira’s medina for Sultan Sidi Mohammed ben Abdallah. The city combines European-style ramparts with Arab-Muslim architecture, earning it UNESCO World Heritage status in 2001. Its port, oriented toward sub-Saharan Africa, long earned it the nickname “Port of Timbuktu.” In late June, the Gnaoua Festival fills the city. Dedicated to Gnaoua music, a Moroccan musical tradition, it also welcomes jazz and reggae: book your accommodations early.

Climb onto the Skala de la Kasbah, the cannon-lined rampart on the medina’s northwestern side: a row of old cannons still points toward the ocean. The platform, accessible at any hour, is a meeting place for the city’s young people. Essaouira’s ramparts served as a filming location for season 3 of Game of Thrones, depicting the fictional city of Astapor. Visit before sunset if you want to enter Bab Ljhad, the northern bastion, which closes at that time.

Blue boats packed along the docks and fishermen mending their nets: Essaouira’s fishing port is first and foremost a working harbor. Carpenters still build wooden boats here, sold throughout Morocco and as far away as France. Sardines and conger eels make up most of the catch. In the market hall at the port entrance, watch the fish auction. Go in the morning, then continue to the Skala du Port, right next door.

There are no signs or audio guides: the Skala du Port, an 18th-century fortified battery, is worth visiting for its cannons and views. From the Borj el-Barmil corner tower, you can see the port and the Mogador Islands, about 1.5 km offshore. These islands form a nature reserve where Eleonora’s falcons, birds of prey, come to breed. In antiquity, King Juba II had purple dye produced here from shellfish. Expect to pay around 60 dirhams; open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The wind is often stronger in the afternoon.

Bayt Dakira, the “House of Memory,” tells the story of Jewish life in Essaouira, a city where Muslims, Jews, and Christians have lived side by side since its founding. It is in the former mellah, the Jewish quarter. Inside are the restored Simon Attias Synagogue, Torah scrolls, silver Hanukkah lamps (for the Jewish Festival of Lights), marriage contracts, and photographs from the 19th and 20th centuries. King Mohammed VI visited in January 2020. Admission is free; closed Saturdays. Clothing that provides coverage is recommended.

activities.text: More interesting than the souvenir stalls, the woodworking shops built into the space beneath the Skala de la Kasbah let you see Essaouira’s artisans at work. They carve thuya, a local conifer whose root wood is used. This craft has been practiced in the medina for centuries. You can watch the wood progress from a rough stump to a finished object.

When the wind blows, as it often does, Essaouira Bay fills with kitesurfing kites. The city is nicknamed the “City of Trade Winds,” after the steady winds that sweep this coast. Partly sheltered by the Mogador Islands, the bay is suitable for beginners: several schools offer kitesurfing, windsurfing, surfing, and stand-up paddleboarding. For your first session, choose a school that provides supervision from the beach and has a rescue boat.
