visits.text: The Chouara Tanneries of Fes are traditional tanneries still in operation - they work with methods unchanged since the 11th century. You see them from the terraces of the leather shops overlooking the vats: take the sprig of fresh mint the shopkeepers offer you at the entrance to soften the smell. In the morning between 8am and 10am, the dyers are at work and the colors are at their brightest.

The Bou Inania Madrasa, built between 1350 and 1357, is open to non-Muslims. Its zellige tilework, carved cedar woodwork and mashrabiya screens are among the finest examples of Marinid art in Morocco. Allow 45 minutes to explore it at a relaxed pace.

The Nejjarine Fountain and its square are the artisan heart of Fes: cabinetmakers work cedar wood in workshops opening onto the alley, and the Wood Museum housed in the adjacent fondouk displays regional crafts across four levels. The museum's terrace offers a plunging view over the medina's rooftops.

The Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque, founded in 859, is considered the world's oldest university still in operation. Not accessible to non-Muslims, but open doors onto the courtyard allow glimpses of the interior from certain adjacent alleys - a fleeting view sufficient to gauge the place's proportions.

The Mellah, Fes' historic Jewish quarter, contrasts with the rest of the medina through its projecting balconies and different facades. The Ibn Danan Synagogue, restored, can be visited. From the Mellah, the gilded Royal Palace Gates are visible at the end of the grand esplanade - the palace itself is not open, but the entry gates are an essential photo subject.

Borj Nord, a 16th-century fortress perched on the hill above the medina, houses the Arms Museum and above all offers the best panorama over Fes el-Bali - the medina sprawls across both valley slopes, with its rooftops, minarets, and the green mass of the Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque at center. See it in late afternoon for the light.

activities.text: Get lost in Fes el-Bali in late afternoon - with its 9,000 alleys, the medina of Fes has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981 and remains one of the largest pedestrian medinas in the Arab world. A local guide for two hours is recommended for the first day: landmarks are virtually nonexistent for uninitiated visitors.
Moroccan cooking class: operators offer morning classes in medina riads - tagine, pastilla, briouats, and mint tea. A 3-hour morning that lets you leave with verified recipes.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes

visits.text: Foum Zguid means “the mouth of the Zguid wadi”; a wadi is a desert watercourse. This small oasis town in Tata Province marks the transition from the Anti-Atlas to the Sahara. Walk in the shade of its palm grove, then visit the remains of the old kasbah on the outskirts. On Thursday mornings, the weekly souk brings the main street to life.

activities.text: You can watch carpet weavers, leatherworkers, and jewelers at work at Foum Zguid’s craft center, which opened in 2022. The town is also the closest to Iriqui National Park, established in 1994 to protect desert wildlife. Its lake, usually dry, filled within a few days after heavy rains in October 2024. No paved road leads there: access is via a dirt track and requires a 4x4 with a driver.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: Gdourt, in the Aït Mansour Gorges, is known for its tightly clustered rammed earth houses clinging to the mountainside above the palm grove. In fall, the palms bear dates; in January–February, the almond trees bloom. Greet residents before photographing them, and stay on the paths, as the gardens are cultivated.

activities.text: At the bottom of an arid red-rock canyon, the Aït Mansour Gorges shelter a palm grove that stays green year-round. Allow two hours to walk along the stream, among date palms, almond trees, and olive trees watered by seguias. In 2018, the FAO, the United Nations food agency, recognized the argan-based agriculture of Aït Souab and Aït Mansour as a globally important agricultural heritage system. The road is paved as far as the entrance to the valley; beyond that, the dirt road may require a 4x4.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: A vertical rock face, carved into strange shapes, borders the river at the bottom of the Oued Laou gorges. The valley is part of Talassemtane National Park, established in 2004. Since 2006, the park has also been part of a UNESCO biosphere reserve, a protected area spanning Morocco and Spain. Barbary macaques, tailless monkeys classified as endangered, frequent these cliffs. Keep your distance and never feed them.

activities.text: Head up the valley on the P4105, a paved road with little traffic, stopping on the shoulders to look at the river. The Moroccan firs that are the park’s reason for being grow much higher up, at elevations between 1,400 and 2,000 m. Here, you are exploring the lower part of the park, shaped by water. The park covers nearly 60,000 hectares, almost six times the area of Paris. Turn back whenever you like to spend the night in Oued Laou.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: At an elevation of about 1,700 m, Igherm is an Anti-Atlas crossroads where the roads from Taroudant, Taliouine, and Tafraoute meet. An agadir, a fortified communal granary, survives on the edge of town, although rebuilding has altered its form. Stop for tea in the center before taking the narrow road down to Tafraoute.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: In Amazigh, the Berber language, Imi n’Ifri means “the mouth of the cave.” This natural bridge, 6 km east of Demnate, is what remains of an enormous cave, most of which has collapsed. Many birds nest in its vaulted ceiling. A trail with about 300 steps leads down to the bottom of the gorge and passes beneath the arch. This section is exposed and has no railing: you need to be sure-footed and comfortable with heights.

Demnate, a small town at the foot of the High Atlas, retains its old ramparts and its kasbah in the center. A large Jewish community lived here from the early 12th century until the late 1950s. It was known for its wine and leatherworking. Olive groves surround the town. If you visit on a Sunday, stop by the weekly souk, where you can find red clay pottery.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: The most beautiful part of Imlil is not its main street, lined with outdoor gear shops, but the terraced orchards surrounding it. At an elevation of 1,740 m, the village is the usual starting point for climbing Toubkal, North Africa’s highest peak at 4,167 m. The September 2023 earthquake hit the valley hard, and reconstruction continues. Toward the end of the day, follow the small irrigation channels that water the terraces: they reveal how these slopes are farmed.

activities.text: Walk uphill from Imlil to the village of Tamatert, at 1,810 m, along a path lined with walnut, apple, and cherry trees. In the surrounding villages, each family tends a few walnut trees. Their walnuts have shells so hard that they are soaked in water for 1 or 2 days so they can be cracked cleanly. If you still have energy, continue to Tizi n’Tamatert Pass, at 2,272 m. Head back down before nightfall: the trails are not lit.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: More than 500 m on a single wave: that’s possible in Imsouane Bay when the swell comes from the right direction. This fishing village has a point break, a wave that consistently forms in the same place and peels along a rocky headland. The bay’s slow, steady wave suits beginners and longboards. The faster wave at La Cathédrale is for experienced surfers only. The bay works best from low to mid tide.

activities.text: Imsouane’s small harbor still relies on fishing: the village boats supply the fresh fish sold on-site. It’s a good stop on the road between Essaouira and Taghazout to watch the surfers and stretch your legs. Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes for the onward drive to Taghazout.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

places.name: Jardin Majorelle

visits.text: To enjoy Majorelle Garden before the crowds, book the first time slot at 8 AM: the site receives more than 700,000 visitors a year. Painter Jacques Majorelle began creating this garden in 1923 and opened it to the public in 1947. He gave his name to Majorelle blue, the intense cobalt blue that covers his villa. Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé bought and restored the property in the 1980s. The fashion designer’s ashes were scattered here in 2008. Tickets are sold exclusively online through the garden’s official website.

The Pierre Bergé Museum of Berber Arts occupies Jacques Majorelle’s former painting studio in the heart of the garden. Opened in 2011, it introduces the Amazigh, the name the Berbers use for themselves, a people who have lived in North Africa for millennia. Its galleries span the Rif to the Sahara, displaying jewelry, clothing, weapons, carved doors, rugs, and musical instruments. One section also explores Berber Jews. Museum admission is separate from garden admission: add it when booking. Open from 8:30 AM to 5 PM.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

map_keywords: Pierre Berge Museum of Berber Arts Marrakech

visits.text: Do not come to the Menara Gardens expecting flower beds: this is a vast olive grove surrounding a pool, with a single, beautiful view. The pavilion with its green tile roof, completed in 1870, is reflected in the water, with the Atlas Mountains in the background on clear days. The pool, built in the 12th century, is elevated, allowing water to flow down to the olive trees by gravity. The water comes from the Atlas Mountains through khettaras, underground tunnels. Admission to the garden is free; the pavilion costs 60 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

activities.text: Catch your breath in Jnan Sbil Garden, created in the 19th century by Sultan Moulay Hassan I. It lies between Fez el-Bali, “Old Fez,” and Fez el-Jdid, “New Fez,” built in the 13th century by the Marinids. Its 7.5 hectares, roughly the equivalent of ten soccer fields, were restored from 2006 to 2010 and reopened in 2011. You will find a large pool, a bamboo garden, and norias, the large wheels that draw water for irrigation. Al Batha Museum is then a 10-minute walk away.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: A broad expanse of water among dry hills, with the High Atlas peaks as a backdrop on clear days: this is Lake Lalla Takerkoust. It is an artificial reservoir. Its dam was built between 1929 and 1935, during the French protectorate, on the Oued N’Fis (oued means river). The water irrigates the Haouz Plain around Marrakech and is also used to generate electricity. Come before 9 a.m. or in the late afternoon, when the lake is calmer and the light on the mountains is softer.

If you have binoculars, follow the western shore of Lake Lalla Takerkoust, the best side for birdwatching. A narrow paved road runs for about 5 km along this shore, with several viewpoints along the way. During the spring and fall migrations, you may spot ruddy shelducks, reddish ducks; black-winged stilts, with their very long legs; or ospreys, birds of prey that dive for fish. Their numbers depend on the water level. A spotting scope makes observing them much easier.

activities.text: Swimming is officially prohibited in Lake Lalla Takerkoust, but you can still head out onto the water. Rental operators along the shore offer pedal boats, small motorboats, and Jet Skis. Some also advertise swimming areas: check the rules on-site before entering the water. The lake is calmer on weekdays. In summer, avoid midday, when the heat is intense and shade is scarce.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: White facades and café terraces: Liberation Square is the lively heart of Larache. The Spanish occupied the city twice, from 1610 to 1689 and then from 1911 to 1956. During the protectorate, they named this square Plaza de España. Its Arab-Andalusian style recalls nearby Andalusia. Have a coffee at an outdoor table and watch the city go about its day.

Pass through Bab el-Medina, the gate opening onto the square, to enter Larache’s medina. Souk Esseghir, the small market, leads to narrow streets that descend to the fishing port. Then return to the central market, 200 m from the square, a renovated covered building in the Andalusian style. Go during the day, when the stalls are at their liveliest.

If you could take away just one view of Larache, it would be the one from Balcon Atlantique. This viewpoint, whose name means “balcony over the Atlantic,” overlooks the ocean. Travel guides rank it among the city’s finest views. Come at the end of the day to watch the sun set over the sea, then walk back to the center.

French writer Jean Genet is buried in Larache’s old Spanish cemetery, at the end of the waterfront promenade. He had lived here for several years and asked to be buried here; he died in 1986. Spanish writer Juan Goytisolo, who died in 2017, is buried in the same cemetery. Be discreet: this is a place for quiet reflection, with no visitor facilities.

activities.text: End the day at Larache’s fishing port, below the medina. The fish landed here help give the city its reputation, along with the region’s oranges and berries. Choose a simple local eatery and ask for the day’s fish, grilled. Confirm the price by weight before it is cooked.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: In 2000, the grounds of Le Jardin Secret were just a pile of rubble divided among more than 130 owners. Yet in the 19th century, one of the medina’s largest riads—houses built around an interior garden—stood here. Caid U-Bihi, a powerful local leader, had it built. Restored with private funding, the site opened to the public in 2016. English landscape designer Tom Stuart-Smith created two gardens here: an Islamic garden with geometric paths lined with citrus trees, and an exotic garden arranged around a large jacaranda tree. Admission is 100 dirhams, free for children under 12.

activities.text: Climb to the top of the tower at Le Jardin Secret for a view over the medina’s rooftops. On your way down, follow the channels and pools in the Islamic garden. They were supplied by khettaras, underground tunnels dug to bring groundwater into the city. These old channels have been restored. The tower ticket costs 40 dirhams in addition to admission. Children under 6 are not allowed in the tower.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: On the hill of Lixus, 80 m above the Loukkos River, the Phoenicians built a city in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. These seafarers came from present-day Lebanon. Follow the path to the temple district, the largest excavated area of the site. The city’s economy depended on salted fish, shipped in amphorae—large earthenware jars whose fragments can still be found. The site is open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., and admission costs 80 dirhams for a foreign adult.

Pliny the Elder, a Roman scholar of the 1st century, placed the Garden of the Hesperides, guarded by a dragon, at Lixus. To him, this dragon was simply a metaphor for the Loukkos River, which snakes across the plain in broad loops. Start at the interpretation center, opened in 2019, where panels help make sense of the rather inconspicuous ruins. Then head uphill to look at the river’s meanders: you will see Pliny’s dragon.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: There are no palaces or gardens here, but faces: the Maison de la Photographie showcases photographs of Morocco dating back to the 1870s. Two collectors, Parisian Patrick Menac’h and Marrakech native Hamid Mergani, assembled these vintage prints. Portraits fill the ground floor. Near the rooftop, a documentary about the High Atlas, filmed by Daniel Chicault in 1956, is screened. Finish on the terrace with a juice or coffee overlooking the rooftops. Open from 9:30 AM to 7 PM; admission is 50 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

activities.text: Leave Marrakech in the morning, heading southwest on the road to Amizmiz. This itinerary does not linger in the city, heading straight for the High Atlas Mountains. Lake Lalla Takerkoust, the first stop, is about 35 km away, a drive of 40 minutes to 1 hour depending on traffic. Fill up before leaving Marrakech and bring supplies for a picnic.

You will head back to Marrakech after spending the morning at Ouzoud Falls. The city is about 150 km away, a drive of 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, or longer if traffic is heavy on the way into Marrakech. Leave Ouzoud in the early afternoon: you will arrive before dark and have time to return your rental car without rushing.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud
High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: Drive from Ouarzazate to Marrakech via the Tichka pass (2,260 m): it is the highest pass on Morocco's national road. The climb is long and the hairpins are many - the landscapes change radically with each altitude. At the top, stop for the view over both sides of the Atlas. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours of driving.

Arrival in Marrakech mid-afternoon. First approach to the medina's ochre ramparts, 19 km long and dating from the 12th century - they give the city that characteristic tint earning it the nickname 'red city'. Settle into a medina riad for total immersion.

The Koutoubia Mosque, built in the 12th century by the Almohads, is one of North Africa's largest mosques with its 70 m minaret - the model for Seville's Giralda. Not accessible to non-Muslims, but the surrounding gardens offer an unobstructed view of the entire tower. Morning recommended for light.

The Bahia Palace, built in the late 19th century by Grand Vizier Si Moussa, extends across 8 hectares of gardens, interior courtyards, and decorated apartments. Its name means 'the brilliant' - the painted cedar ceilings, mosaics, and moucharabiehs justify the appellation. Visit is self-guided, allow 1 hour.

The Saadian Tombs, rediscovered in 1917 beneath a layer of plaster, house the sepulchers of 66 members of the Saadian dynasty including Sultan Ahmad al-Mansour (died 1603). The main hall, decorated with 12 Carrara marble columns, is a jewel of Hispano-Moorish art. Arrive at opening (9am) to avoid the line.

The Majorelle Garden, created from 1923 by a French painter and purchased in 1980 by a couturier who saved it from destruction, is Morocco's most visited garden. The intense cobalt blue of the structures - christened 'Majorelle blue' - contrasts with the green of bamboos and cacti. Book online: capacity is limited and queues without reservation are long from 10am. Arrival at opening recommended.

The fashion and art museum adjacent to Jardin Majorelle traces the history of a great French couture house through its archives, sketches, and a selection of iconic pieces. The building's architecture in ribbed red brick is itself remarkable.

Marrakech's Mellah, historic Jewish quarter adjacent to the royal palace, preserves ancient synagogues and distinctive architecture with its overhanging balconies. The Lazama Synagogue, from the 16th century, is the most accessible and best preserved.

activities.text: First evening on Jemaa el-Fna square: at nightfall, the square transforms into a permanent spectacle - storytellers, snake charmers, Gnawa musicians, orange juice stands, and smells of grilled skewers. It's been UNESCO-listed as intangible cultural heritage since 2001. Arrive at 7pm to watch the square gradually come alive.

Dive into Marrakech's souks: each street has its specialty - leather, spices, babouches, brass, carpets. The dyers' souk (Souk des Teinturiers) is most spectacular, with wool skeins hanging from facades in red, yellow, and violet. Bargaining obligatory and advised with a smile.

Traditional hammam in late afternoon: medina hammams offer the complete package - steam, scrubbing with kessa glove, black beldi soap, and argan oil massage. Allow 1.5 hours. A way to close two days of walking through the souks.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes

activities.text: In summer, Martil Beach receives up to 80,000 people a day, according to the official beach survey. This seaside resort is the closest to Tetouan, northeast of the city. Its sand stretches for 4 km to the mouth of the Martil River, which the Spanish called Río Martín. Walk along the waterfront, then rejoin the coastal road heading southeast.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: Small but exquisite, the Al-Attarine Madrasa may be the day’s loveliest surprise. Allow 30 minutes to visit. Its name comes from the adjacent Al-Attarine souk, the spice and perfume market. The Marinid sultan Abu Said Uthman had it built from 1323 to 1325. Look at the bronze-clad cedar entrance doors: they are copies, since the originals are preserved at the Al Batha Museum. Upstairs are around thirty student rooms. Admission is 20 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Ben Youssef Madrasa, a former Quranic school that housed students, is the largest in Morocco. The Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib completed it in 1564–1565. Its 130 rooms surround a courtyard where a shallow pool reflects the carved facades. The school could accommodate up to 800 students. Head upstairs to see how cramped the rooms are, with light coming in from the courtyard. Closed in 2018 for restoration, the madrasa reopened in April 2022. It is open daily from 9 AM to 7 PM; admission is 50 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: From floor to ceiling, no wall is bare in the Bou Inania Madrasa, a religious school that housed its students. At the bottom is zellige, a mosaic of small, colorful ceramic tiles; above it is carved plaster; higher still is carved cedar. Sultan Abu Inan of the Marinid dynasty had it built from 1350 to 1355. It is the only madrasa in Morocco that also served as a congregational mosque for Friday prayer. Its prayer hall, reserved for Muslims, can be seen from the courtyard. Admission is 20 dirhams; it closes during prayers, with a longer closure on Fridays.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Road from Chefchaouen to Meknes with a stop at Volubilis, Morocco's largest Roman site: 42 hectares of UNESCO-listed ruins, founded in the 3rd century BCE. At its peak, the city had between 10,000 and 20,000 inhabitants. The Arch of Caracalla (early 3rd century CE), the Villa of Venus mosaics, and the forum are the centerpieces. Go before 10am - after that, the heat is punishing and there's no shade on site.

3 km from Volubilis, the holy village of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun clings to two hills shaped like camel humps. This is the resting place of Idris I, founder of Morocco's first Muslim dynasty and the country's first Islamic king. Every summer, for more than a month, the village hosts the Moussem (pilgrimage) of Moulay Idriss, one of the most important in Morocco.

Meknes, nicknamed the city of the 'Moroccan Louis XIV': Sultan Moulay Ismail made it his capital from 1672 and endowed it with 40 km of ramparts pierced by 20 monumental gates. Bab Mansour, main gate to the imperial city, is one of Morocco's most imposing. The Mausoleum of Moulay Ismail, open to non-Muslims, is a masterpiece of zellige and stucco.

activities.text: Evening stroll through Meknes' medina: less touristy than Fes or Marrakech, it has retained an authentic character with its butchers, grocers, and artisans working in their shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes

visits.text: In the mid-15th century, the Jews of Fez settled beside the Royal Palace in the Mellah neighborhood. The word means “salty place,” perhaps because of a saltwater spring or a former salt warehouse. On Rue Bou Khessissat, opened in 1924, Jewish houses have balconies facing the street. The Ibn Danan Synagogue, dating from the late 17th century, reopened in 1999 after restoration. From its roof, you can see the white tombs of the Jewish cemetery. Admission prices vary: ask on arrival.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: The Mellah, Marrakech’s former Jewish quarter, begins at Place des Ferblantiers. Artisans still make metal lanterns by hand in this square. The neighborhood emerged in the mid-16th century, next to the royal kasbah. It had around 40,000 residents in the late 1940s. Today, around 200 Jews remain in Marrakech. In the narrow streets east of the main street, look for the small Stars of David on doors and grilles. The neighborhood is free to explore: ask before photographing residents.

activities.text: Shop for spices at the Mellah’s covered market, where stalls display ground spices in tall pyramids. The secret behind these perfect cones is a metal mold hidden inside. Look for ras el-hanout, a spice blend whose recipe varies from shop to shop. It often contains white pepper, ginger, turmeric, and cumin. Cumin is the main spice grown around Marrakech: choose round seeds, a sign of quality.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Road from Fes to Merzouga via the Ziz Valley and Midelt: the route crossing the Tizi n'Talrhmt pass (1,907 m) is one of the most spectacular passages in the Middle Atlas. As altitude descends, vegetation disappears and the ochre and red tones of the pre-Sahara take over. Arrival in Merzouga early afternoon.

First contact with Erg Chebbi in late afternoon: the dunes stretch 22 km long and 5 km wide, with peaks reaching 150 m. It's one of the most imposing dune systems in the Moroccan Sahara. Sunset transforms the golden sand into a palette of red, orange, and violet - climb the nearest dune to the village to watch the transformation.

Sunrise from the summit of a dune: wake before dawn (allow 20 minutes minimum climbing) to be in place when light begins grazing the dune crests. The contrast between shadow and light on the waves of sand is the most photographed moment in the Moroccan Sahara. After sunrise, the desert's silence reclaims its dominion.

Lake Dayet Srij, at the dunes' edge, is a seasonal lake that forms after rains and attracts flamingo colonies. Depending on season, birds are visible to the naked eye from the shore. The village of Khamlia, a few kilometers from Merzouga, is inhabited by a Gnawa community whose percussion music is played evenings.

activities.text: Camel ride to a bivouac in the open desert: local operators offer 1.5 to 2-hour round-trip packages by camel to reach a camp at the foot of the great dunes. Berber dinner, percussion music around the fire, and night under the stars. It's an experience that requires advance planning - book through your Merzouga riad or guesthouse upon arrival.

Quad or 4x4 in the dunes during morning: operators offer one- or two-hour circuits through Erg Chebbi's secondary dunes, with access to zones usually inaccessible on foot. The experience is radically different from camel riding.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes

visits.text: “M’Hamid of the gazelles”: the name M’Hamid El Ghizlane recalls the gazelles that once lived on the nearby plains. The last oasis along the Drâa before the desert, it was long a stop for caravans crossing the Sahara. Several ksour, fortified earthen villages, lie hidden in its palm grove, including M’Hamid Bali and Ouled Driss. Most are almost empty and crumbling. Ask before entering a house: some require a small contribution.

The modest ruins of Ksebt El Allouj in M’Hamid are worth visiting mainly for the history they evoke. They are generally dated to the Saadian dynasty, which ruled Morocco in the late 16th century, when the oasis depended on trade across the Sahara. No one knows exactly what the building was used for. Make it the destination of a short walk through the palm grove, with a local resident as your guide.

activities.text: You will leave your rental car in M’Hamid El Ghizlane, where the N9 ends. The 50 to 60 km leading to Erg Chigaga consist entirely of unpaved tracks across stony plateaus, ancient dry lake beds, and soft sand where vehicles easily get stuck. Book a 4x4 with a driver and an overnight stay at an organized desert camp, a tent camp run by a tour operator, in advance. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours for the journey.

The sand begins right at the edge of M’Hamid El Ghizlane: small dunes are within walking distance or a short dromedary camel ride away. At sunset, their crests turn orange as the palm grove falls into shadow. It is a good warm-up before Erg Chigaga. Set out an hour before sunset and return before it is completely dark.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: The religious and scholarly heart of Fez since the 9th century, Al Quaraouiyine Mosque stands at the center of the medina. According to tradition, Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy merchant from Kairouan, Tunisia, founded it around 857 or 859. Al Quaraouiyine University grew around this mosque. Guinness World Records describes it as the oldest educational institution still operating in the world. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims. Through an open doorway, you can glimpse part of the courtyard: stay on the threshold and avoid prayer times.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: “The booksellers’ mosque”: that is what Koutoubia means, a name recalling the booksellers’ souk that once surrounded it. Its 77 m minaret, completed in the late 12th century, serves as a landmark in the medina. Each of its four faces has a different arrangement of decorative arches: walk around it to compare them. On the esplanade, you can see the foundations of an earlier mosque. It is believed to have been replaced around 1158 because it was incorrectly aligned toward Mecca. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims: you can view the exterior free of charge.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Al Batha Museum of Islamic Arts occupies Dar Batha Palace, the sultans’ summer residence in the late 19th century. Converted into a museum in 1915, it reopened on February 26, 2025, after six years of restoration. Among its roughly 700 works, look for the minbar from the Mosque of the Andalusians, a carved wooden pulpit more than a thousand years old from which the imam preaches. The Andalusian garden, designed in 1915, is divided into four sections around a fountain. Admission is 60 dirhams, with opening hours from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except Tuesdays; allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: As early as 1711, traveling merchants slept upstairs at the Nejjarine fondouk and stored their goods on the ground floor. A fondouk was a merchants’ inn built around a courtyard. Since 1998, the building has housed the Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts. Inside, you will see carved doors, musical instruments, and wooden tablets made by students at the Quranic school. In the courtyard, the large scale was used to weigh goods. The museum is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Finish at the rooftop café, with views over the medina’s roof terraces.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Seen from the street, the facade of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum resembles fabric: its terracotta bricks form a woven pattern. Designed by the French firm Studio KO, the building opened in October 2017, just steps from Majorelle Garden. The permanent gallery displays around fifty haute couture pieces. They are rotated regularly to preserve them. The museum is open from 10 AM to 6 PM and closed on Wednesdays. Book a combined ticket with the garden on the official website.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Calm water on one side, Atlantic breakers on the other: Oualidia’s lagoon is protected from the ocean by a sandbar. At low tide, the water recedes and sandy islets emerge. The beach along the lagoon offers sheltered swimming areas, and Moroccan families come here for their summer vacations. Stay on the lagoon side: facing the ocean, the shore break—the first waves near the shore—is dangerous even in mild weather.

Oualidia takes its name from Sultan El Oualid of the Saadian dynasty, who had a kasbah built in 1634 to defend the entrance to the lagoon. Along the waterfront, a palace built around 1940 for the future King Mohammed V now stands abandoned. It still belongs to the royal family, however. You can view its arcaded galleries from the beach. Take this short walking loop in the late afternoon, after your swim.

activities.text: “Oysters taste best when eaten right in the water,” says an Oualidia guide quoted in the Moroccan press. Oyster farming was introduced here in 1956. Pacific oysters are raised in beds recognizable by their wooden stakes. Beach shacks serve the oysters raw, with lemon. They are also the town’s main export.

If you visit between fall and spring, Oualidia’s lagoon fills with birds arriving to spend the winter or stopping along their migration routes. It is part of the Sidi Moussa-Oualidia Ramsar site, a wetland protected by an international convention since 2005, where 114 species of waterbirds have been recorded. Small boats follow the shores, where you can see gray herons, spoonbills, egrets, and flamingos stopping between Spain and Senegal.

You can also explore Oualidia’s lagoon at your own pace in a kayak or on a stand-up paddleboard rented on the beach. Sheltered by the sandbar, the water stays calm, which is reassuring for beginners. On the ocean side, a beach shack also rents surfboards. Go in the morning, when the beach is quieter.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: Stop in the Dadès Gorges en route from Merzouga: the pink limestone cliffs close in on the road until forming a vertiginous corridor. At the gorges' entrance, the 'monkey fingers' - rock formations eroded into grotesque bulbs - are one of the strangest landscapes in pre-Saharan Morocco. Allow 30 to 40 minutes.

The ksar of Aït Ben Haddou, 30 km from Ouarzazate, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987. This fortified village in pisé and raw earth, built from the 17th century on the trade route between Sudan and Marrakech, has served as a backdrop for some twenty Hollywood films - Gladiator, Game of Thrones, Lawrence of Arabia. Climb to the collective granary (agadir) atop the ksar for panorama over the Ounila Valley.

The Kasbah Taourirt, built in the 19th century for the powerful Glaoui tribe, dominates Ouarzazate from downtown. A section is open for visits: stucco-decorated apartments, interior courtyards, and terraces offer a glimpse of Berber luxury of the era. Allow 45 minutes.

Excursion south into the Draa Valley: from Ouarzazate, the valley stretches for 200 km through palm groves, pise villages and kasbahs. The road first crosses the Jbel Saghro by the Tizi n'Tinififft pass, then reaches the valley at Agdez: from there the finest landscapes begin - palm trees, market gardens, and kasbahs appearing at every bend in the road. Allow a full-day round trip from Ouarzazate.

activities.text: Dinner on a terrace in Ouarzazate facing the Atlas: the city, at 1,160 m altitude, marks the frontier between mountains and desert. The Draa Valley palm groves begin here.

Visit the Atlas Studios of Ouarzazate: one of the world's largest open-air filming complexes, used since the 1960s for productions from Lawrence of Arabia to Babel. Guided tours access sets still standing - Jerusalem, Rome, or Egyptian ruins in papier-mâché amid the desert. It's kitschy but fascinating.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes
Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: Five kilometers of sand between the mountain and the sea: welcome to Oued Laou Beach. The town, 44 km from Tetouan, relies mainly on fishing outside the summer season. In summer, vacationers arrive and festivities bring the town to life. Walk along the sand to the river mouth, where the Oued Laou River flows into the sea.

activities.text: The best meal in Oued Laou is a plate of grilled sardines. The Moon guide describes this fishing port as a quiet town where people eat sardines and tagines. Settle into a small restaurant near the port and ask for the catch of the day. On Saturday, browse the souk, the weekly outdoor market.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: The Oumesnat Traditional House is a former family home turned living museum in the Ammeln Valley, about 6 km from Tafraoute. Arranged on several levels around a central kitchen, it shows how local people lived in the 18th and 19th centuries. The owners often lead the tours, which have an admission fee. To get there, leave the main road and follow the dirt road toward Jbel Lekst and the signs for “Maison Traditionnelle.”

Oumesnat’s lanes climb the mountainside between rammed earth houses, some partly carved into the rock. Higher up, the ruins of the old village crumble on the slope. In January–February, almond trees bloom all around. After visiting the Traditional House, climb through the lanes before getting back on the road to Taroudant.

activities.text: Take one of the trails starting in Oumesnat, such as the “Lion’s Head” loop. This name refers to the rocky flank of Jbel Lekst, a 2,359 m peak with the Ammeln Valley stretching out at its foot: seen from a particular spot on the road, it forms the shape of a lion’s head. The trail offers sweeping views of the valley, which has about twenty Berber villages. Bring water and sturdy shoes, as the slopes are steep.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: You hear Ouzoud Falls before you see them: their roar rises from the gorge as soon as you reach the first viewpoints. The water drops about 110 m in several tiers before flowing into the gorge of the Oued el-Abid, the river below. A maintained trail from the village of Tanaghmeilt leads to the foot of the falls in 15 to 20 minutes. There is no official admission ticket. Arrive early in the morning: it gets very crowded in summer.

Ouzoud is thought to come from an Amazigh word meaning “olive,” and olive trees do indeed surround the falls. About ten small traditional olive oil mills still operate along the river. Stop at one on your way down to Ouzoud Falls: it is a chance to see an old-fashioned mill at work, just steps from the water.

activities.text: Climb into one of the small shared boats waiting at the foot of Ouzoud Falls. Local operators steer them across the pool to get as close as possible to the main falls. From below, you get a better sense of the water’s 110 m drop. There is a charge for the ride: agree on the price before boarding, and put your phone in a waterproof pouch.

If you encounter Barbary macaques around Ouzoud Falls, do not feed them. They are a protected species and the only monkeys living in the wild in Morocco. Feeding them disrupts their natural behavior. To watch them, follow the loop trail that crosses the river at the foot of the falls and takes about 1 hour. Keep your bags and food securely closed.

The trail through the Oued el-Abid gorges is worth the effort: it takes you far from the crowds gathered near Ouzoud Falls. The falls plunge into these gorges, and the site is part of the M’Goun UNESCO Global Geopark. A geopark is an area recognized for the richness of its rocks and landscapes. These trails are less traveled than the area around the falls: go with a licensed local guide and plenty of water.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: Look up in every room of Bahia Palace, whose name means “the Brilliant”: its painted cedar ceilings are the highlight of the visit. Grand Vizier Si Moussa, the sultan’s prime minister, began construction in the 1860s. His son Ba Ahmed expanded it until 1900, bringing the palace to around 150 rooms. The grand courtyard, measuring 50 m by 30 m, is paved with Carrara marble. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the palace is still undergoing restoration. Open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Badi means “the Incomparable,” yet all that remains of this palace are immense earthen walls surrounding pools and gardens. Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour began building it in 1578. He likely financed it with the ransom paid by Portugal, which Morocco defeated that year. The Italian marble used for the columns was traded for its weight in sugar. Around 1707, Sultan Moulay Ismaïl had the palace dismantled to reuse its materials in Meknes. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the site reopened as early as October. Admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: If you arrive early, you will have the gates of the Royal Palace of Fez, known as Dar al-Makhzen, almost to yourself. The palace covers 80 hectares, the equivalent of more than a hundred soccer fields. It is not open to visitors. Its seven gates on Place des Alaouites were built from 1969 to 1971. Their gilded bronze doors are covered in geometric patterns and framed by blue zellige and carved cedar. Photograph the gates, but not the guards, and do not get too close.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Jemaa el-Fna square changes throughout the day. In the morning, orange juice vendors, snake charmers, and artists working with henna, a plant-based dye applied to the skin, set up in the half-empty square. Around 4 p.m., cooks assemble their stalls. At sunset, musicians and Berber troupes draw crowds, often until around 1 a.m. In 2001, UNESCO recognized the square for its storytellers and street performers. For a view of it all from above, head to a café terrace at the edge of the square.

activities.text: Have dinner on the benches at Jemaa el-Fna’s food stalls, which light up as night falls. Try snail soup, skewers, tagine, or fried fish. Choose a busy stall, eat with bread instead of utensils, and drink bottled water. Arrive early in the evening to find a seat. The French Ministry for Foreign Affairs reports bag and phone thefts in Marrakech: keep your valuables close to you.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: The ringing of hammers on copper guides you to Seffarine Square. Its name means “coppersmiths,” the artisans who work copper. Their workshops were documented here as early as the 16th century. Even today, they hammer out large cauldrons here. Seffarine Madrasa, built in 1271, also opens onto the square: it is Morocco’s oldest building originally constructed as a madrasa. It still houses students and is not open to visitors. Settle beneath the old tree to watch the artisans, and ask before photographing a workshop.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Thirteen hairpin turns and a climb of about 750 m over 19 km: the road from Lake Lalla Takerkoust up to the Kik Plateau must be earned. It first crosses dry hills, then winds upward to an elevation of about 1,320 m. Stop at one of the final bends wherever the shoulder allows: the lake comes into view below. This climb is well known among cyclists, so take care on the curves.

Moulay Brahim overlooks the gorges that bear its name, along the road descending from the Kik Plateau toward Asni. This holy village is clustered around the mausoleum of Moulay Brahim and draws many visitors from Marrakech. The shrine is a place of prayer: view it from the lanes without trying to enter. Farther down, Asni holds its weekly souk on Saturdays. If you pass through that day, stop for 1 hour to browse the stalls.

activities.text: Park on the Kik Plateau and walk for 1 to 2 hours among wheat fields and villages. The earthen Berber houses follow the mountain slope and blend into it. On the paths, donkeys and mules remain the surest way to reach the hamlets. In spring, snowmelt brings the meadows into bloom. The villages are very modest: bring water and a picnic, and always ask before photographing anyone.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: Walls painted blue and white line the narrow streets of the Kasbah of the Oudayas, the citadel overlooking the mouth of the Bouregreg River. Enter through Bab Oudaia, a gate carved between 1195 and 1199 for Sultan Yacoub el-Mansour of the Berber Almohad dynasty. In the 17th century, Moriscos, Muslims expelled from Spain, settled here and founded a republic of privateers that attacked merchant ships. Rue Jamaa leads to the semaphore platform, a former station that sent signals to ships. Come early, before the tour groups.

More recent than it looks, the Andalusian Garden of the Oudayas was created between 1915 and 1918. This was the beginning of the Protectorate, the period when France administered Morocco (1912–1956). With its bougainvillea and citrus trees, the garden imitates those of Al-Andalus, medieval Muslim Spain. Nearby Café Maure offers a chance to take a break on the terrace. Save this garden for the middle of the day, between the kasbah and the medina.

Rabat’s medina, the old city surrounded by ramparts, is best explored without a fixed plan. Its Rue des Consuls, laid out in the 17th century, housed major merchants and foreign delegations until 1912. Farther along, Souk as-Sabbat is nicknamed the street of shoes. To the southwest, the Mellah was the neighborhood where Jewish families traditionally lived. Allow 1 hour to wander: the Kasbah of the Oudayas is just a few minutes away on foot.

Though unfinished, Hassan Tower is even more impressive than a completed minaret. Sultan Yacoub el-Mansour began construction in 1196 for an enormous mosque, but work stopped when he died in 1199. The tower reaches 44 m, instead of the planned height of more than 60 m. Inside, ramps replace stairs: the muezzin, the man who calls people to prayer, was meant to be able to ride up on horseback. The rows of columns in front mark the prayer hall, ruined by the earthquake of 1755. From the center, allow 30 minutes for the uphill walk, or take a petit taxi.

If you enjoy ceremonies, watch the royal guards on horseback outside the Mausoleum of Mohammed V: they generally agree to be photographed. Completed in 1971, this white marble monument with a green roof was designed by Vietnamese architect Cong Vo Toan. It houses the tombs of Mohammed V, a hero of independence, his son Hassan II, and Prince Moulay Abdallah. Non-Muslim visitors view the tombs from an interior balcony. Cover your shoulders and knees; the tourist office lists weekday opening hours as 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Chellah brings together two eras across 7 hectares above the Bouregreg River. Below, Sala, an ancient Roman city, preserves the remains of its forum, a temple, and a triumphal arch. Higher up lies the Marinid necropolis, the cemetery of a dynasty that ruled Morocco during the Middle Ages. Enter through a gate completed in 1339. Storks nest on the minaret. Eels live in a pool: according to a local belief, feeding them helped women have children. Following restoration, the site reopened in 2024: 70 dirhams, or 120 with an audio guide.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

activities.text: Cumin, saffron, and paprika add color to the stalls of Rahba Kedima, a small, sunny square amid the souks. It is also known as Spice Square. Shops around its edges sell spices, traditional cosmetics, and herbal remedies. Some offerings are surprising, such as dried lizards. In the center, women sell woven baskets and cotton caps. Several cafés line the square, making it an ideal place to take a breather away from the narrow passageways.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: It is best to visit Safi’s National Ceramics Museum before Potters’ Hill: you will then understand what you are looking at. The museum occupies the Kechla, a fortress listed as a historic monument, and its terrace offers views over the city. Its seven rooms trace Moroccan ceramics from prehistory to the end of the 20th century, from the Rif Mountains to the High Atlas. One room honors Boujemaa Lamali, a master potter associated with the pottery school that opened in Safi around 1920. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; closed Tuesdays.

activities.text: Earthen kilns and their chimneys rise across Safi’s Potters’ Hill, visible from the Bab Chaaba gate at the edge of the medina. This neighborhood, listed as a historic monument since 1920, houses cooperatives where artisans mainly preserve traditional techniques. Safi is renowned for its blue ceramics. Walk among the workshops and watch the potters throw pots—that is, shape clay on a wheel.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: A contemporary art garden in the Ourika Valley may come as a surprise, but Anima Garden makes the combination work. Austrian artist André Heller opened it in 2016, 27 km south of Marrakech. Plan a round-trip drive from Setti Fatma to visit the garden. Across three hectares, ceramic sculptures and pools mingle with plantings, with the Atlas Mountains as a backdrop. Arrive when it opens, at 9 a.m., to enjoy the peace and quiet. Admission is around 140 dirhams per adult: check the price before you go.

activities.text: Setti Fatma’s first waterfall is only the beginning: the seven-waterfall hike takes more effort higher up. The village, deep in a gorge, is the last in the Ourika Valley accessible by paved road. A steep trail leads to the base of the first and largest waterfall in twenty minutes. Another ten minutes of almost vertical climbing brings you to a viewpoint with a refreshment stand. It takes another hour of effort to reach the highest waterfall. Avoid weekends and summer, when residents of Marrakech flock here.

In the Ourika Valley, a village’s name can tell you its market day: Tnine Ourika comes from tnine, meaning “Monday” in Arabic. This is where the valley’s large weekly souk takes place every Monday. Farther up the valley, Aghbalou hosts a smaller market on Thursdays. From Setti Fatma, plan to drive down the valley to reach these markets. If you are visiting on either day, set aside an hour to browse the stalls, preferably in the morning.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: A golden sand beach stretching as far as the eye can see and a white tomb facing the ocean: Sidi Kaouki takes its name from this marabout, the tomb of a local saint. Every August, a moussem, a festival honoring the saint, brings this small Berber village 25 km south of Essaouira to life. The rest of the year, the atmosphere remains peaceful despite the surf schools. Swim with caution: the ocean here is often rough, with strong currents.

activities.text: In Sidi Kaouki, you will find schools renting boards and wetsuits for beginners and experienced surfers alike. The beach break works almost year-round, with the biggest swells arriving in winter. Suitable for beginners, it works best around high tide. From September to March, conditions are better for surfing. From April to October, the steady wind tends to attract kitesurfers and windsurfers.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: If you visit the dyers’ souk before noon, you will see artisans working over their vats. Skeins, those long loops of wool, dry above the alley in yellow, blue, or red. Natural colors come from saffron, indigo, poppies, or cochineal, a small insect that is crushed. Many workshops now use chemical dyes. Admission is free: turn down anyone claiming that a guide is required. A close-up photo of an artisan often costs 10 to 20 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

activities.text: The best part of Marrakech’s souks is wandering without a particular destination. Start at the northeast corner of Jemaa el-Fna and head up to Souk Semmarine, the main covered passageway. Its slatted roof, once made of reeds, is now metal to reduce the risk of fire. Farther along, the passage branches off toward other souks, each originally associated with a trade: leather, metalwork, jewelry, or carpets. Bargain with a smile, but never go back on an agreed price.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: The Mellah’s loveliest surprise is hidden behind an unmarked door: Lazama Synagogue (Slat al-Azama). According to tradition, it was founded in 1492 by Jews expelled from Spain. A courtyard tiled in blue and white leads to the prayer hall. There, zellij mosaics made from glazed terra-cotta tiles form a Star of David. The rooms around the courtyard tell the story of Jewish life in Morocco. Visit Sunday through Thursday: during Shabbat, access is reserved for worshippers.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: In 1984, Belgian artist Jean Vérame painted blue a group of large granite boulders rounded by erosion, south of Aguerd Oudad, near Tafraoute. The colors have faded over time, and most of the rocks have since been repainted. The blue contrasts with the pink granite and pale sand. Come early in the morning: the low-angle light brings out the colors, and the heat is still bearable.

Pink granite mountains surround Tafraoute, a small Anti-Atlas town at an elevation of about 1,000 m. Its name comes from the Amazigh word tafrawt, meaning “basin” and, by extension, “valley.” In the center, a small market sits on a knoll overlooked by a minaret, amid renovated lanes. The town is liveliest on Wednesday, the main market day.

activities.text: Walk south from Tafraoute toward the village of Aguerd Oudad, overlooked by a granite rock nicknamed Napoleon’s Hat: its silhouette resembles the emperor’s bicorne, a two-pointed hat. The path follows a dry riverbed to the painted rocks. Farther on, vegetation takes over the riverbed: head back up to the small road at that point. Allow a good two hours and wear closed-toe shoes.

Tafraoute bills itself as the capital of the Berber babouche, a round-toed leather slipper that is often brightly colored. Shops in the center sell them alongside amlou, an almond and argan oil spread that is a regional specialty. Taste the amlou on a piece of bread before buying. For babouches, try several sizes and take your time bargaining.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: Locals call the rock at the end of the beach south of Taghazout Imouran, meaning “the dying”; it is also nicknamed Devil’s Rock. According to oral tradition, fighters killed battling the Portuguese in the 16th century are said to have been buried there. This Berber fishing village, 19 km north of Agadir, saw hippies arrive in the late 1960s, followed by surfers. The beach stretches for about 7 km to the rock: set out early if you want to walk its length.

Anchor Point, 3 km north of the village of Taghazout, is a long wave that peels along a rocky headland. With a good swell, it continues as far as the Hash Point surf spot and ends on Panoramas Beach. Conditions are best from September to April. Even if you’re not surfing, settle on the rocks to watch the surfers, keeping out of their way.

activities.text: Take your first surf lesson in Taghazout, where schools and rental shops line the village. To get started, choose a sandy beach over a rocky point like Anchor Point: the bottom is less dangerous if you fall. The region’s waves are best from September to April. Allow half a day for travel, getting equipped, and the lesson.

To find out where argan oil comes from, visit a production workshop around Taghazout: alongside fishing and tourism, it is one of the village’s sources of income. The argan tree grows wild in southwestern Morocco. The know-how associated with it, passed down mainly by women, has been on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2014. The fruit is harvested and dried, the pits are cracked, and the kernels—the seeds inside—are ground before the paste is kneaded with warm water.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: Residents call it the “village bank”: the agadir of Aït Kine, a fortified communal granary a ten-minute drive from Tleta Tagmoute, still stores barley, dried fruit, and valuable documents. Archives document its use as early as 1708. Each family has its own room, 76 in total, plus a room reserved for the tribe. A caretaker opens the door at dawn and closes it at sunset: come during the day and ask him for a tour.

activities.text: Park upstream from the Tleta Tagmoute oasis and continue on foot: the seguias, small irrigation canals, guide you from one plot to the next. Pomegranate and olive trees grow beneath the date palms, with grains, vegetables, and alfalfa for livestock in their shade. This layered planting protects the lower crops from the scorching sun. Allow forty-five minutes for the walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

activities.text: “The Great Climb”: that is what Talaa Kebira means, the sloping street linking Bab Bou Jeloud to the heart of the medina of Fez. There are no cars here: the medina is one of the largest urban pedestrian zones in the world. Goods travel on donkeys or handcarts, so give them the right of way. Farther down, look for the mosaic-decorated minaret of the Chrabliyine Mosque. Shops nearby still sell traditional shoes. Take your time wandering and compare prices before buying.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: A 13th-century Quran copied onto gazelle skin is the centerpiece of the library at the Naciria Zawiya in Tamegroute. A zawiya is the headquarters of a Sufi brotherhood, part of a mystical tradition within Islam, and also serves as a place of teaching. This one dates back to 1575 and still holds several thousand manuscripts on medicine, mathematics, and astrology. Access depends on the caretaker being present: ask in Zagora before setting out, and put your camera away, as photography is generally prohibited.

activities.text: No two pots are quite the same green: in Tamegroute, the shade of the glaze, a coating that turns glassy during firing, varies with the heat of the kiln. The village potters still fire their pieces in traditional kilns, and local tradition traces this craft back to Fez. Step into a workshop to watch the pottery being thrown, then compare the shades before buying. On Saturdays, the village souk also displays their pottery.

You will see your first dunes a few kilometers south of Tamegroute, at Tinfou. They are much smaller than those of Erg Chigaga, but offer enough sand for a first barefoot walk. Stop for half an hour in the early afternoon, then set off again to reach M’Hamid before nightfall: driving at night is discouraged in Morocco.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Tangier Ibn Battouta Airport, southwest of the city. Tangier deserves a trip of its own: on this itinerary, its airport serves only as the starting point for the Atlantic coast. Before signing the rental agreement, ask how much it costs to drop off the car in Al Hoceima. The route ends nearly 300 km from Tangier, on the Mediterranean.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: Arrival in Tangier and first immersion in the medina: the Grand Socco, former marketplace, marks the crossroads between the colonial town and the old city. The Kasbah, perched atop the medina, houses the Dar el Makhzen - the former sultan's palace converted into a museum, displaying Roman mosaics and ethnographic collections. Climb to the terrace: the view sweeps across the Strait of Gibraltar and, on clear days, the Spanish coastline.

14 km west of Tangier, Cap Spartel is the extreme northwestern point of continental Africa: this is where the Mediterranean and Atlantic meet before your eyes. The lighthouse dates from 1864 - climb to the platform to watch the two seas merge into one. The sight is more impressive than you'd imagine.

5 km from the cape, the Caves of Hercules open onto the Atlantic through a fissure whose shape eerily resembles the map of Africa. The site has been occupied for over 7,000 years BCE - archaeologists found stone tools here. According to legend, Hercules rested here before completing his eleventh labor. Come early morning to avoid the crowds; entry opens at 9am.

activities.text: Wander the medina's alleys in late afternoon: the souks come alive, the scents of spices mingle with those of warm bread, and shopkeepers close up for the day. This is when Tangier reveals its true character, far from organized tours.

Mint tea at Café Hafa, perched on a cliff overlooking the strait since 1921: generations of writers and artists have set down their notebooks here facing the horizon. Settle on the terrace to watch ferries pass between two continents.
After the caves, walk along Achakkar Beach at the foot of the cliffs: it's a wild, uncrowded beach where you can stroll along the rocks. A good contrast to the bustle of Tangier's port.

visits.text: Climb to the terrace of a leather shop for an overhead view of Chouara Tannery, the largest of Fez’s three tanneries. The hides first soak in white vats containing water, salt, lime, and pigeon droppings: the ammonia in the droppings softens the leather. They then move into the dye vats, with poppy red, indigo blue, or henna orange. Access to the terrace is free, but leave 10 to 20 dirhams if you do not buy anything. If someone tells you “the tannery is closed today,” it is a trick to take you elsewhere.

visits.text: Taroudant’s kasbah, the former royal quarter in the northeast of the city, was built in the 17th century by Sultan Moulay Ismaïl. Enter through Bab Sedra, its old gate, to explore a quiet residential neighborhood. Near Bab el Kasbah, you can climb onto the ramparts for a view over the city. In the evening, residents stroll through the park in front of the kasbah.

Mint tea on a café terrace and street performers in the late afternoon: Assarag Square is the heart of Taroudant. Between it and Talmeklat Square, the covered lanes of the craft souk bring together potters, jewelers, coppersmiths (artisans who work with copper), and carpet sellers. Take time to compare before buying, and always negotiate the price.

The smell reaches you before the sight: the Bab Targhount tannery processes hides just outside Taroudant’s ramparts. Around forty tanners prepare sheep, goat, and dromedary camel hides as visitors watch. Nearby shops sell bags, poufs, and sandals made on-site. Hold a mint leaf under your nose if the smell bothers you.

activities.text: Take a horse-drawn carriage ride around Taroudant’s ramparts late in the day, when the sun warms the ocher walls. These 7.5 km of earthen walls date mainly from the 16th century and the Saadian dynasty. They have earned the city its nickname, “Little Marrakech.” Agree on the price before getting in: the hourly rate is negotiable.

Few souvenirs, plenty of life: Taroudant’s Amazigh souk, the municipal market, mainly sells spices, dried fruit, and household goods. In its open-air section, artisans turn old tires and plastic into saddles, watering troughs, and baskets for donkeys. Enter from Assarag Square. Watch without getting in the way, and ask before taking photos.

visits.text: Built from local earth, Tata’s ksour blend into the landscape. These fortified villages of rammed earth recall the city’s past as a caravan crossroads. Tata’s workshops keep basket weaving, carpet weaving in warm colors, and local pottery traditions alive. Wander through them in the morning before temperatures rise: in summer, they can exceed 45 °C.

activities.text: Beneath the Agadir Lhena palm grove, north of Tata, water flows through khettaras, underground channels that bring groundwater to the gardens. A water clock, or clepsydra, is still used to divide irrigation time among the plots: each family receives water for a measured period. To get there, turn left just after the ford, the crossing through the wadi, drive to the end of the village, then continue on foot along the palm grove trail.

Climb to the highest point in the village of Agadir Lhena for a sweeping view of the Tata oasis. Palm groves line the Tata wadi, a tributary of the Drâa, at the foot of Jbel Bani, the long rocky ridge bordering the southern Anti-Atlas. A series of oases stretches from Agadir Lhena to Tiguisselt. Go up in the late afternoon, when the light is softer and the heat has subsided.

visits.text: Behind crumbling earthen walls, the kasbah of Télouet hides reception rooms adorned with zellige (mosaics of small glazed tiles), carved stucco (plaster sculpted in relief), and painted cedar ceilings. The Glaoui family began building it around 1860. In 1893, a snowstorm stranded the army of Sultan Hassan I nearby. Madani El Glaoui supplied the court for several weeks and later became grand vizier, the equivalent of a prime minister. Since the 2023 earthquake, only some of the rooms have been open to visitors, with a guide included in the admission ticket.

activities.text: Télouet’s salt mines partly explain the Glaoui family’s wealth. Their kasbah stood on one of the main caravan routes between Marrakech and the southern valleys on the edge of the Sahara. Salt traveled alongside other goods. Near the village, a salt mine is still operating and can be visited. Ask in the village or check with your kasbah guide for directions.

places.name: Tetouan

visits.text: Small but complete: that is how UNESCO describes Tetouan’s World Heritage–listed medina. After the Reconquista, the reconquest of Spain by Christian monarchs, refugees expelled from Andalusia rebuilt the city. A wall roughly 5 km long surrounds it, with seven gates. Follow the main streets connecting these gates: they lead to squares, mosques, and artisan quarters. An official guide will save you unnecessary detours.

Smaller and less colorful than those in Fez, Tetouan’s tanneries make no attempt to impress. A tannery is a workshop where animal hides are processed into leather in vats. This one dates to the late 15th or early 16th century. Look for the small door to the left of Bab Mkabar, one of the medina’s gates, and keep a few dirhams handy for a tip.

“The cleanest and best built”: that was explorer Charles de Foucauld’s assessment of Tetouan’s mellah in 1883. A mellah is the former Jewish quarter of a Moroccan city. This one had as many as six thousand Jewish residents in the late 19th century. Look for its houses with second-floor balconies and paired pointed-arch windows, which distinguish it from the rest of the medina.

An old bastion, a defensive structure built around 1830 above the Bab el-Okla gate, houses Tetouan’s ethnographic museum. It reopened in January 2022. Ethnography studies ways of life: here, clothing, jewelry, and instruments tell the story of daily life in the city. One room presents the squndo, a 15th-century water distribution network that served the medina. Finish in the small garden, with views of the city and the Rif Mountains.

Step inside the School of Arts and Crafts, just outside Bab el-Okla. Founded in 1919 under the Spanish protectorate, it trains artisans in Moroccan and Andalusian crafts. Since 1928, it has occupied a richly decorated building surrounded by a garden. Visit Monday through Friday, as the school does not receive visitors on weekends; on Fridays, it takes a long midday break.

If Lixus left you wanting more, Tetouan’s archaeological museum rounds out the visit. It displays mosaics, Latin inscriptions, and amphorae from Lixus and Tamuda, another ancient city in the region. A scale model depicts the M’Zora cromlech, a circle of large standing stones in northern Morocco. The museum is open Wednesday through Monday; allow time for its Arab-Andalusian garden.

The Ensanche, the new town built by the Spanish west of the medina, is a reminder that Tetouan was the capital of the Spanish protectorate from 1913 to 1956. Residents call it Chanti. Its five-story buildings have stores on the ground floor. The Church of Our Lady of Victories, consecrated in 1925, dominates Moulay el-Mehdi Square. Finish on pedestrian-only Mohammed V Avenue, where cafés and used-book sellers bring the street to life in the evening.

Trains no longer stop at Tetouan’s old station, yet people still come through its doors. The Modern Art Center has occupied the building since 2013. It mainly showcases contemporary Moroccan and Andalusian artists, and its temporary exhibitions can be worth a detour. Admission is free. It is open Tuesday through Saturday, with a midday break: come in the morning or late afternoon.

activities.text: Crisp on the outside and fragrant with lemon inside: that is Tetouan-style pastilla. Pastilla is an oven-baked pie made with very thin sheets of dough and a meat filling. In Tetouan, it is prepared with chicken, eggs, and lemon. Order it at a restaurant in the medina and share it with a group, as it is filling.

visits.text: The water is salty, yet palm trees grow all around: the Tissint waterfalls tumble over rocks in the heart of the oasis. You can swim here to cool off; keep your sandals on, as the wet rock is slippery. The village’s name is also familiar to scientists. In July 2011, a meteorite that fell 48 km to the south was identified as a piece of the planet Mars, thanks to gases from the Martian atmosphere trapped inside the rock.

Disguised as a Jewish traveler, French explorer Charles de Foucauld stayed in Tissint while exploring Morocco. His account, Reconnaissance au Maroc, published in 1888, earned him the gold medal of the Société de géographie. A village guide can take you to his poorly maintained house, about 400 m downstream from the spring. The route passes through the old village’s covered alleys, sheltered from the sun.

visits.text: Tizi n’Tichka Pass was long listed at 2,260 m, but a GPS measurement taken in 2022 puts it at about 2,205 m. It remains the highest of North Africa’s major road passes. The French army laid out the road in the 1930s along an old caravan trail. Its name means “pass of the pastures” in Tamazight, the Berber language. On a clear day, the view stretches as far as Toubkal. From December to March, snow can close the road: check the weather before setting out.

activities.text: Stop in Taddert, a village beside the N9, roughly halfway between Marrakech and Ouarzazate. Travelers stop here for a bite to eat or to browse local crafts before tackling Tizi n’Tichka Pass. The road has been modernized and is much safer than it once was. The curves and trucks still demand attention: take a break here if you have been driving since morning.

visits.text: End the weekend on the hill of the Marinid Tombs, an eight-minute walk from Borj Nord. The entire medina of Fez stretches out before you, with its tightly packed houses and minarets. This 14th-century necropolis is attributed to the Marinids, the dynasty that built the Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas. Two tall, ruined mausoleums with large horseshoe arches remain. Access is free, with no facilities: bring water. Come with others and take a petit taxi back down before nightfall, as thefts have been reported here in the evening.

visits.text: If you arrive at the Saadian Tombs when they open, around 9 a.m., you will have a shorter wait to see the Hall of the Twelve Columns. This royal necropolis was built primarily by Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour, who died in 1603. His tomb lies in this hall, beneath twelve columns of Carrara marble, a white marble from Italy. Later, Sultan Moulay Ismaïl walled up most of the entrances. The French historic monuments service rediscovered the site in 1917, then opened it to the public. The rooms are viewed from behind barriers. Admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

visits.text: Five watchtowers, attributed to the Portuguese by the Moroccan National Tourist Office, gave the village of Torres de Alcala its name. Torres means “towers” in Spanish. You are in Al Hoceima National Park, established in 2004, which protects 50 km of coastline and part of the sea. Climb up to the ruins for a view of the bay, then head down to the pebble-and-sand beach at the mouth of the Beni Boufrah River.

A rocky islet 500 m offshore encloses the bay of Cala Iris, a few kilometers to the west. The small port shelters around thirty fishing boats. The islet is part of the national park: it is one of the few places where the ferruginous limpet, an endangered shellfish that clings to rocks, survives. Do not collect anything from the rocks, and swim at the beach of sand mixed with pebbles.

activities.text: If you still have energy, follow the coastal trail east from Cala Iris. Reaching the area around Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera requires a long hike: allow enough time for the round trip. This rock has belonged to Spain since 1564. In 1930, an earthquake connected it to the coast with an 85 m sandbar. Directly opposite stood Badis, the port that served the inland city of Fez from the 14th to the 16th century. If you do not have enough time for the round trip, walk along the trail for 30 minutes to enjoy the coastal views, then retrace your steps.

visits.text: A paradise that depends on rain: in summer, the river in Paradise Valley runs low and the greenery fades. This valley along the Tamraght River (locally, rivers are called oueds), in the foothills of the High Atlas, is lined with palm trees and clear pools where you can swim. From the parking lot, an easy trail reaches the pools in about 30 minutes. Ideally, visit in late winter or early spring, when the river is full.

activities.text: You can extend your Paradise Valley walk by following trails that climb above the cliffs along the Tamraght River. Wear shoes with ankle support and bring plenty of water. Avoid jumping from rocks into the pools when the water is low: accidents have happened here. To continue to Imouzzer des Ida Outanane, plan a round-trip drive from Paradise Valley, followed by a walk to the waterfalls. In this village perched at 1,250 m, the falls flow mainly from January to March.

visits.text: “Timbuktu 52 days”: Zagora’s famous sign showed how long it took to reach this city in Mali across the Sahara, on foot or by dromedary camel. The original has been replaced by a mural, but the old sign still exists. Stop for a photo as you enter town: it is the most evocative reminder of the caravan era.

Amezrou Kasbah is worth a detour precisely because people still live there. In Zagora’s palm grove, you enter through a maze of narrow streets where families live. The path leading there follows a canal shaded by palm trees. Be discreet and do not photograph residents without their permission.

activities.text: Hike up Jbel Zagora, the mountain overlooking the city, on a 3.8 km loop. Allow nearly two hours for about 250 m of elevation gain over rocky terrain, with white arrows marking the way in places. At the foot of the mountain stand the remains of a fortress built by the Almoravids, a medieval Berber dynasty. Set out early and bring water: from the summit, at 966 m, the view takes in Zagora and the Drâa palm grove.

visits.text: If you see passersby ducking under a beam across the alley, you are approaching the Moulay Idriss II zawiya. A zawiya is a shrine built around a saint’s tomb. These beams mark the boundary of the holy site: until 1912, non-Muslims and pack animals were not allowed to pass beyond them. The tomb belongs to Idriss II, who ruled from 807 to 828 and is traditionally considered the founder of Fez. The interior is reserved for Muslims: approach the doors without photographing worshippers.
